## Introduction

[`targets`](https://docs.ropensci.org/targets/) is a package for R that manages a workflow in an R-native manner. It reduces the unnecessary rerunning of computationally heavy analyses after editing code, while ensuring that all affected downstream analyses are rerun.  

`targets` keep track of input files, intermediate R objects, functions and reports using hashes and time stamps. It builds a pipeline using the file `_targets.R`, which is the primary file for editing your workflow. In this file, *targets* are defined as individual commands, and the dependency between commands are evaluated when the pipeline is visualized or run. Individual *targets* are saved and metadata is written to enable tracking whether they have changed since the last run.

## Demo repository

I have made a repository for use during the RSE tech group presentation. It can be cloned for testing `targets` on your own computer. The demo is performed using a Docker container which is available at jenfransson/rse_targets:latest, which was built using the files in the repository.

[https://github.com/jenfransson/rse_targets/]

## Installation

### Installation with pixi (written by Claude)

Install R and the packages with [Pixi](https://pixi.prefix.dev/).

```{.bash}
pixi init targets-demo
cd targets-demo
pixi add r-base r-targets r-tarchetypes r-crew r-readr r-ggplot2 r-visnetwork
```

::: {.callout-note}
On `osx-arm64`, the conda-forge `r-base64url` package (a dependency of `targets`) ships without its compiled library, and loading `targets` fails with ``shared object ‘base64url.so’ not found``. Fix it with `pixi run Rscript -e 'install.packages("base64url")'`. `linux-64` is unaffected.
:::


### Other options

`targets` can also be installed from CRAN (`install.packages("targets")`) or renv (`renv::install("targets")`). In the demo repository, I installed it using renv in the rocker/rstudio based on the repository's `renv.lock` file.


## Getting started

To create a new targets project, navigate to a new folder (or `demo` in the repository) and start R. Then run:

```

library(targets)
use_targets()

```

This creates a new file called `_targets.R`, which is the main home for your pipeline-generating code<1>. It contains example code as well as comments about how to edit it.

## `_targets.R`

`_targets.R` has four main parts:

* Normal R code
    * Load any packages that are required to read the pipeline (not to run it), including `targets`
    * Set any global R options
* `tar_option_set()`
    * Define options for targets, such as packages needed to run the targets' commands and parallel computing options
* `tar_source()`
    * Source all .R-scripts in R/ as well as any other specified files
* Target list
    * The file ends with a list of `tar_target()` calls or other similar functions
        * `tarchetypes` provides other useful target-defining functions such as `tar_quarto*` and `tar_render*`
    * This list defines all of the targets that will be considered when building the pipeline
    * Any target defined in this list can be accessed in other targets' commands
    * The order of the targets does not matter

## Testing and running the pipeline

`targets` includes functions to visualize and run the pipeline. This is done outside of the `_targets.R` file, such as in the console or another script.

### `tar_make()`

`tar_make()` is the function called to evaluate and run the pipeline. Once started, the pipeline will be constructed from `_targets.R` and all input files and dependencies will be checked. If the pipeline can be constructed without errors, all outdated targets will be regenerated. During the run, the progress will be printed, but the verbosity can be adjusted using the `reporter` parameter. 

If you don't want to use the default settings of basing the pipeline on `_targets.R` and 

Note: Whether a target should be rerun or not is finally evaluated once all upstream targets have been checked and rerun (if needed). This means that in a default run, if a target was rerun due to e.g. a change to the command but the final object has the same hash, the downstream targets will not be rerun.

### `tar_visnetwork()`

`tar_visnetwork()` is the main function that I use for checking the status of my pipeline. It generates a DAG, with each function and target colored according to whether they are outdated or not, or if they have errored. This graph quickly becomes messy once you have a decent number of targets, but it is interactive so you can zoom and highlight individual targets.

## Example

```

# Load packages
library(targets)

# Set up targets
use_targets()

# Visualize pipeline
tar_visnetwork()

# Run pipeline
tar_make()

# Visualize pipeline
tar_visnetwork()

# Read the target "model"
tar_read(model)

# Load the target "data" and examine it
tar_load(data)
head(data)

```

Edit _targets.R as you wish and examine the results using `tar_visnetwork` and `tar_make`


## `targets` outputs

All *targets* defined with tar_target() are stored in `_targets/objects` after creation<1>. The format of the output can be defined in the tar_target() function but is RDS by default. In addition, metadata including the hash of the object is stored in `_targets/meta/meta`. Changing or removing the files or editing the corresponding metadata will cause the *target* to be considered outdated and force it to be rerun in the next run.



## Footnotes

1. Default settings such as `_targets.R` containing the pipeline script and `_targets` being the `targets` store can be changed using `tar_config_set()`

























## Key takeaways

- What decides whether a target reruns? Its code, its dependencies, or its input files changing. (`tar_outdated()` lists them.)
- Write each step as a function, and keep `_targets.R` as the wiring.
- `pattern = map(x)` replaces a loop with one tracked target per element.
- What changes when you move from laptop to HPC? The controller, not the pipeline.
